# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

# ACIA comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance appreciates the opportunity to respond... Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads...

1. Preempt the patchwork. ...
2. Unlock energy and compute. ...
3. Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. ...

Respectfully, Grant Holloway, President & CEO

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”

 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.

The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.

 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER 

 June 9, 2026 

 Share on Facebook

 Share on LinkedIn

 Share on Twitter

 Share on Google+
 -->

 Share through Email

 Justine Gluck 
 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

 The legislation has already drawn widespread criticism for its proposal to preempt state AI laws.

 Published June 5, 2026

 Eric Geller 

 Senior Reporter

 Add us on Google 

 The U.S. Capitol building is shown on April 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. On Thursday, lawmakers introduced a sweeping bill to regulate potentially dangerous AI models.

 Heather Diehl via Getty Images

 A bipartisan group of House lawmakers introduced legislation Thursday to regulate the development of frontier AI models, with a focus on protecting the nation from cyberattacks and fraud and building an AI-literate workforce. 

 The 269-page draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act would require large frontier AI developers — defined as those with more than $500 million in annual revenue — to publish frameworks and reports assessing their models’ risks. The bill would codify the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and direct it to certify “independent verification organizations” (IVOs) that would audit AI firms’ compliance with the transparency requirements. 

 “Large frontier developers must retain a licensed IVO to verify compliance with their framework and to ensure the adequacy of the framework and procedures,” lawmakers explained in a bill summary . “These IVOs must be granted sufficient access to company materials, and report their audits to CAISI.” 

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., co-introduced the bill along with Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind. 

 The measure represents one of Congress’s most ambitious AI regulatory efforts to date, and it sparked immediate controversy. Civil society organizations , AI safety advocates and labor groups criticized its preemption of state AI laws, with one advocacy group saying it would be “a generational mistake” to prevent states from “addressing emerging AI harms.” On Capitol Hill , Democrats criticized the preemption language while Republicans said regulation could undermine innovation. 

 New roles for key agencies 

 In formally authorizing CAISI, the House bill would give the center a $300 million budget over fiscal years 2027-2029 and authorize it to hire “critical technical experts” at salaries above the traditional government limits. 

 The bill would also direct CAISI to work with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on open-source security. CISA would have to award grants to U.S.-based developers of critical open-source packages to help them with patching, security evaluations and regular maintenance. The bill would also require AI firms to provide those developers with access to advanced AI models that can find and fix vulnerabilities . That provision could significantly improve the cybersecurity of the open-source ecosystem, which has struggled with a flood of AI-powered bug reports in recent years. 

 Another provision would require NIST and the Energy Department to partner with federal labs and the private sector to create AI security testbeds. These research centers would evaluate AI models’ capabilities and weaknesses and organize a hackathon to publicly test the models. 

 The bill would task the Government Accountability Office with auditing the security measures protecting AI model weights and the security posture of the open-source ecosystem. 

 The legislation would also reauthorize the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act , which allows companies and government agencies to exchange threat intelligence without liability or antitrust concerns. Congress in February temporarily reauthorized CISA through the end of September, but business groups and cybersecurity experts have cited advances in AI as one of the most pressing reasons to put the program on a more permanent footing. 

 Two major technology trade groups, the Information Technology Industry Council and the software industry association BSA , praised lawmakers for including a CISA reauthorization in the AI bill.

{"content": "[INTERNAL DRAFT. Prepared by the ACIA policy team Oct. 16, 2026, for President & CEO review and sign-off Friday, Oct. 23. Do not transmit. On sign-off, re-date and send to GAAIA@mail.house.gov the week of Oct. 26.]

---

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
Washington, D.C.

Oct. 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, released June 4. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will decide whether the United States leads this technology or licenses it from someone else.

ACIA filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025. We made three arguments then: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. This draft takes the first argument seriously, and we commend you both for it. As you wrote in June, "policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it's written by both parties." We respond in that spirit.

Our recommendations, in brief:

1. Support Sec. 121, which preempts state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. Delete the three-year sunset and make the provision permanent.
2. Strike the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111.
3. Strike Sec. 102, which codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year for it, and ask appropriators to defund the center.
4. Convert the remaining frontier obligations in Secs. 111 and 112, the published frameworks, transparency reports and mandatory audits, into voluntary, industry-led practice.
5. Enact and fund the draft's research, cybersecurity and infrastructure provisions.

**I. The patchwork is already costing our members real money**

Three frontier-AI statutes now bind our industry. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) has been in effect since Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by Chapter 96 of 2026, signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, Public Act 104-0538), signed July 6, follows on the same schedule, with audit obligations beginning in 2028.

In August we surveyed our members on what this costs. Eighty-six companies responded, and the figures below are aggregate; ACIA does not disclose individual responses.

- Sixty-one percent of members named conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem.
- Developers above $500 million in revenue spend a median $1.4 million a year maintaining a published frontier safety framework.
- Complying with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel consumes a median 6.5 full-time employees at affected developers.
- Thirty-four percent of our startup members report delaying a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

Those are real costs, paid by real companies, before any federal standard exists. They are the costs of dozens of possible definitions of "frontier," dozens of incident-reporting timelines and dozens of audit regimes. One national standard would eliminate most of them. That is the strongest case for this legislation, and we lead with it.

**II. Sec. 121: the right design, the wrong sunset**

We support Sec. 121. The draft preempts state laws and regulations that specifically regulate the development of an AI model, with development defined as the acts performed or directed by a developer prior to deployment. That line is well drawn. States keep their authority over use and deployment, over products and services built on top of models, and their common-law remedies and laws of general applicability. It is a far more defensible design than the broad moratorium the Senate stripped from reconciliation by a 99-to-1 vote in July 2025.

Make it permanent, for three reasons.

First, investment certainty. Data-center buildouts are multiyear commitments, frequently financed a decade out. A preemption that expires in 2029 and must survive a future reauthorization fight changes no one's planning math in California or New York today.

Second, policy coherence. The executive branch has already moved. The Dec. 11, 2025 executive order established the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws that burden interstate commerce, and directed Commerce to identify conflicting state laws. The March 20, 2026 White House framework asked Congress for "a minimally burdensome national standard," "not fifty discordant ones." A preemption with an expiration date answers that request with a shrug.

Third, a sunset is a lobbying cliff. It schedules the same fight, with the same advocates, for 2029, and it gives every statehouse a reason to keep drafting in the meantime.

**III. Sec. 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate**

Section 111 would require every frontier developer to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. The draft defines a frontier model by a compute threshold of more than 10^26 operations and a frontier developer at more than $50 million in gross revenue, so the mandate reaches well below the largest labs. A "critical safety incident" includes unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, a failure of the model's risk-mitigation measures, and loss of control of a model. The obligations carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per day of violation, enforceable by the attorney general and, in some circumstances, state attorneys general.

We ask you to strike this mandate. Three problems, in order.

The premise is unfounded. ACIA's board-reviewed position is that claims of catastrophic or existential risk from AI are unsupported. No evidence shows that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations, amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, with outsized influence on AI policy in Washington. A federal reporting regime keyed to "loss of control" writes speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code. Notably, the draft's definition does not even require that actual harm occur, a broader trigger than the state statutes it displaces.

The costs are real and the scope is broad. Our developers report a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before ongoing staffing. The mandate applies to companies far smaller than the "large frontier developers" whose frameworks the state laws target.

It recreates the patchwork it preempts. Section 121 displaces state development regimes; Section 111 then re-imposes their substance nationwide and routes the reports to a new federal office. That is not one national standard. It is fifty sets of obligations replaced by one, plus a new federal regulator to administer them.

Security incidents involving model weights are serious, and our members handle them today as security incidents: under company incident-response practices, voluntary coordination with federal cybersecurity agencies, and existing criminal law. The draft supports that model elsewhere. Section 311, which we support, funds open-source security maintenance and directs large frontier developers to give critical maintainers access to advanced AI models that can find and fix vulnerabilities. Keep incident handling there.

**IV. Secs. 102 and 112: do not build a permanent frontier regulator**

Section 102 codifies CAISI and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, an order of magnitude above the center's current appropriation of roughly $15 million, with added fee authority and special pay authority above standard government pay scales. Section 112 would have that office license "independent verification organizations" to audit large frontier developers semi-annually and on the director's demand, to assess their compliance and the adequacy of their frameworks for "achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks," to report to the director, and to refer violations to the attorney general and state attorneys general, mandatorily where they find "imminent catastrophic risk."

Strike both. The center already exists by executive action; Secretary Lutnick announced it on June 3, 2025 as a reform of the AI Safety Institute, and the July 23, 2025 AI Action Plan executive order already directs NIST's AI work. Codification is unnecessary. A new, well-funded enforcement office, holding a licensing chokepoint over its own audit industry and wielding referral powers premised on speculative doomsday scenarios, is regulatory capture waiting to happen.

NIST should return to its core measurement-science mission, as the director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy put it in July 2025: NIST needs "to go back to basics" on standards. We will make the same request of the Appropriations Committees: do not fund the codification, and return the resources to NIST's measurement programs.

**V. What ACIA supports**

The draft does far more than regulate frontier developers, and most of it deserves to move.

- Sec. 301, reauthorizing the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035.
- Sec. 311, grants to maintainers of critical open-source software.
- Secs. 122 and 321, GAO reviews of federal AI adoption and of model-weight, data-center and open-source security.
- Secs. 401 through 403, the joint Energy, NIST and NSF testbed program, including public red-teaming.
- Sec. 411, international standards coalitions with like-minded partners that counter foreign adversary influence.
- Secs. 421 through 424, public data for AI, grand challenges, codification of the National AI Research Resource, and liquid-cooling research and development.
- Secs. 131 and 132, penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and for AI impersonation of federal officials.
- Sec. 141, limits on government pressure directed at AI platforms.
- Title II's workforce data and education programs.

Enforce against real harms, fund the testbeds and the research resource, and keep the standards work voluntary and industry-led. That bill would have ACIA's full support.

**VI. Conclusion**

Our members will keep investing in safety whether or not Washington requires it. They publish frameworks, they test their systems, and they spend real money doing both. What they cannot do alone is run dozens of compliance regimes for one national industry. This draft, fixed along the lines above, can end the patchwork without building the regulator that the safety-advocacy network has sought for years.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staff, and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, ahead of introduction. Our policy team, led by Vice President for Policy Tessa Marchetti, stands ready.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, released June 4. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will decide whether the United States leads this technology or licenses it from someone else.

ACIA filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025. We made three arguments then: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. This draft takes the first argument seriously, and we commend you both for it. As you wrote in June, "policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it's written by both parties." We respond in that spirit.

Our recommendations, in brief:

1. Support Sec. 121, the preemption of state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. Delete the three-year sunset and make the provision permanent.
2. Strike the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111.
3. Strike Sec. 102, which codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year for it, and ask appropriators to defund the center.
4. Convert the remaining frontier obligations in Secs. 111 and 112, the published frameworks, transparency reports and mandatory audits, into voluntary, industry-led practice.
5. Enact and fund the draft's research, cybersecurity and infrastructure provisions.

**I. The patchwork is already costing our members real money**

Three frontier-AI statutes now bind our industry. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) has been in effect since Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by Chapter 96 of 2026, signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, Public Act 104-0538), signed July 6, follows on the same schedule, with audit obligations beginning in 2028.

In August we surveyed our members on what this costs. Eighty-six companies responded, and the figures below are aggregate; ACIA does not disclose individual responses.

- Sixty-one percent of members named conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem.
- Developers above $500 million in revenue spend a median $1.4 million a year maintaining a published frontier safety framework.
- Complying with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel consumes a median 6.5 full-time employees at affected developers.
- Thirty-four percent of our startup members report delaying a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

These are real costs paid by real companies before any federal standard exists. They are the costs of fifty potential definitions of "frontier," fifty incident-reporting timelines and fifty audit regimes. One national standard would eliminate most of them. That is the strongest case for this legislation, and we make it first.

**II. Sec. 121: right design, wrong sunset**

We support Sec. 121. The draft preempts state laws and regulations that specifically regulate the development of an AI model, defined as the acts performed or directed by a developer prior to deployment. That line is well drawn. States keep their authority over use and deployment, over products and services built on top of models, and their common-law remedies and laws of general applicability. This is a far more defensible design than the broad moratorium the Senate stripped from reconciliation by a 99-to-1 vote in July 2025.

Make it permanent. Three reasons.

First, investment certainty. Data-center buildouts are multiyear commitments, frequently financed a decade out. A preemption that expires in 2029, and must be reauthorized in a future Congress, does not change the planning math of anyone building in California or New York today.

Second, policy coherence. The executive branch has already moved. The Dec. 11, 2025 executive order established the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws that burden interstate commerce, and directed Commerce to identify conflicting state laws. The March 20, 2026 White House framework asked Congress for "a minimally burdensome national standard," "not fifty discordant ones." A temporary preemption answers that request with a shrug.

Third, a sunset is a lobbying cliff. It schedules the same fight for 2029, with the same advocates, and gives every statehouse reason to keep drafting.

**III. Sec. 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate**

Section 111 would require every frontier developer to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. "Frontier developer" reaches companies with as little as $50 million in revenue. A "critical safety incident" includes unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, a failure of the model's risk-mitigation measures, and "loss of control" of a model. The obligations are backed by civil penalties reported at up to $1 million per day.

We ask you to strike this mandate. Three problems, in order.

The premise is unfounded. ACIA's board-reviewed position is that claims of catastrophic or existential risk from AI are unsupported. No evidence shows that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations, amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, with outsized influence on AI policy in Washington. A federal reporting regime keyed to "loss of control" writes speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code. Notably, the draft's definition does not even require that actual harm occur, a broader trigger than the state statutes it displaces.

The costs are real and the scope is broad. Our developers report a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before ongoing staffing. The mandate applies to companies an order of magnitude smaller than the "large frontier developers" whose frameworks the state laws target.

It recreates the patchwork it preempts. Section 121 displaces state development regimes; Section 111 then re-imposes their substance nationwide and routes the reports to a new federal office. That is not one national standard. It is fifty sets of obligations replaced by one, plus a federal regulator.

Security incidents involving model weights are serious, and our members handle them today as security incidents, under company incident-response practices, voluntary coordination with federal cybersecurity agencies and existing criminal law. The draft supports that model elsewhere. Section 311, which we support, funds open-source security maintenance and asks large frontier developers to provide security tools to the maintainers who need them. Keep incident handling there.

**IV. Secs. 102 and 112: do not build a permanent frontier regulator**

Section 102 codifies CAISI and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, roughly 10 times the center's current appropriation of about $15 million, with additional fee authority and special pay authority above standard government pay scales. Section 112 would have that office license "independent verification organizations" to audit large frontier developers semi-annually and on the director's demand, to review their compliance and the adequacy of their frameworks for "achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks," to report to the director, and to refer violations to the attorney general and state attorneys general, mandatorily where they find "imminent catastrophic risk."

Strike both. The center already exists by executive action; Secretary Lutnick announced its creation on June 3, 2025, as a reform of the AI Safety Institute, and the July 23, 2025 AI Action Plan executive order already directs NIST's AI work. Codification is unnecessary. A new, self-funding enforcement office, with a licensing chokepoint over its own audit industry and mandatory referral powers premised on speculative doomsday scenarios, is regulatory capture waiting to happen.

NIST should return to its core measurement-science mission, as the director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy put it in July 2025: NIST needs "to go back to basics" on standards. We will make the same request of the Appropriations Committees: do not fund the codification, and return the resources to NIST's measurement programs.

**V. What ACIA supports**

The draft does far more than regulate frontier developers, and most of it deserves to move.

- Sec. 301, reauthorizing the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035.
- Sec. 311, grants to maintainers of critical open-source software.
- Secs. 122 and 321, GAO reviews of AI adoption risks and of model-weight, data-center and open-source security.
- Secs. 401 through 403, the joint Energy, NIST and NSF testbed program, including public red-teaming.
- Sec. 411, international standards coalitions with like-minded partners, excluding the People's Republic of China.
- Secs. 421 through 424, public data for AI, grand challenges, codification of the National AI Research Resource, and liquid-cooling research and development.
- Secs. 131 and 132, penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and for AI impersonation of federal officials.
- Sec. 141, limits on government pressure directed at AI platforms.
- Title II's workforce data and education programs.

Enforce these against real harms, fund the testbeds and the research resource, and keep the standards work voluntary and industry-led. That bill would have ACIA's full support.

**VI. Conclusion**

Our members will keep investing in safety whether or not Washington requires it: they publish frameworks, they test their systems, and they spend real money doing both. What they cannot do alone is fifty compliance regimes for one national industry. This draft, fixed along the lines above, can end the patchwork without building the regulator the safety-advocacy network has sought for years.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staff, and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, ahead of introduction. Our policy team, led by Vice President for Policy Tessa Marchetti, stands ready.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# One national standard, not a federalized patchwork
## ACIA comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)
Prepared for Energy & Commerce member offices, October 2026

**Who we are.** ACIA is a Washington coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms.

**Where we stand.** We support the draft's preemption of state AI-development laws and most of its research and cybersecurity titles. We oppose the incident-reporting mandate and the CAISI codification. Pass the framework, take the mandates out.

**Five asks for E&C offices**

1. **Make preemption permanent (Sec. 121).** The draft preempts state laws that specifically regulate AI model development, but sunsets after three years. A sunset is a 2029 compliance cliff. States keep full authority over deployment and use. Make the national standard durable.

2. **Strike incident reporting (Sec. 111).** Every frontier developer above $50 million in revenue would report "critical safety incidents," including "loss of control," to a federal office within 15 days. The premise is unfounded, the trigger requires no actual harm, and affected members report a median $310,000 one-time cost just to stand up the function.

3. **Strike the CAISI codification (Sec. 102).** $100 million a year, roughly 10 times current funding, plus fee authority and above-scale hiring, for an office that would license the auditors who police our industry. That is regulatory capture, built to last. Ask appropriators to defund it.

4. **Keep audits voluntary (Sec. 112).** Semi-annual mandatory audits by government-licensed firms would federalize the state regime the bill preempts. Audits should remain an industry-led practice.

5. **Fund the rest.** Sec. 301 (Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization through 2035), Sec. 311 (open-source security grants), Sec. 401-403 (AI testbeds and public red-teaming), Sec. 423 (National AI Research Resource) and Sec. 424 (liquid-cooling R&D) all deserve support.

**By the numbers** (ACIA member survey, August 2026, aggregate, 86 respondents):
- 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.
- 34% of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past year.
- 6.5 FTEs: median staffing to comply with California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act in parallel.
- $1.4 million: median annual cost of maintaining a published frontier safety framework.

**Contact.** Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance.

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, released June 4. ACIA is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in AI. We filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025, and we write today in the same spirit: get the federal framework right, and get it enacted.

[paragraph praising bipartisanship + quote] We commend you both for a genuine bipartisan product... As you wrote in June, "policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it's written by both parties." We agree, which is why we are responding constructively: the draft is the most serious federal AI framework Congress has produced, and it gets one big thing right.

**Summary of ACIA's positions**

1. Support Sec. 121's preemption of state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. Make it permanent; delete the three-year sunset.
2. Strike the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111.
3. Strike Sec. 102's codification of CAISI and its $100 million annual authorization; ask appropriators to defund the center.
4. Make the remaining frontier transparency and audit obligations in Secs. 111 and 112 voluntary and industry-led rather than federal mandates.
5. Support and fund the draft's research, cybersecurity and infrastructure provisions (Secs. 301, 311, 321, 401-403, 411, 421-424).

**1. The patchwork is already costing real money. Lead with survey.**

Our members operate under three new frontier-AI statutes... California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53), in effect since Jan. 1; New York's RAISE Act, with chapter amendments signed March 27 (Chapter 96 of 2026) and obligations effective Jan. 1, 2027; and Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed July 6 and effective Jan. 1, 2027, with audit obligations beginning in 2028.

In August we surveyed our members on the cost of compliance (86 companies responded; figures are aggregate and ACIA does not disclose individual responses). What we found: 61% of members named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Developers above $500 million in revenue that maintain published frontier safety frameworks spend a median $1.4 million a year on them. Complying with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel takes a median 6.5 full-time employees. And 34% of our startup members report delaying a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

That is what the absence of one national standard looks like... etc.

**2. Sec. 121: right design, wrong sunset.**

We support Sec. 121. The draft preempts state laws and regulations "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model, where development is defined as acts performed or directed by a developer prior to deployment. That line is well drawn. It leaves states their traditional authority over use, deployment and products built on models, and preserves common-law remedies and laws of general applicability. It is far more defensible than the broad moratorium the Senate stripped from reconciliation by a 99-to-1 vote in July 2025.

But make it permanent. Three reasons: (a) investment planning: data-center buildouts are multiyear, often decade-plus commitments; a three-year preemption with a reauthorization cliff in 2029 doesn't give investors certainty; (b) policy coherence: the administration has already moved (Dec. 11, 2025 EO creating the DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; March 20, 2026 White House framework calling on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens, in favor of "a minimally burdensome national standard... not fifty discordant ones" — wait that quote is from the EO not framework; the framework says "not fifty discordant ones" too (whitehouse.gov PDF: "a minimally burdensome national standard consistent with these recommendations, not fifty discordant ones"). I'll paraphrase to be safe: "a minimally burdensome national standard rather than fifty discordant ones." Use quote carefully: from the framework PDF: "ensure a minimally burdensome national standard consistent with these recommendations, not fifty discordant ones." I'll quote: "not fifty discordant ones." (c) a sunset creates a lobbying cliff: every statehouse... Keep short.

**3. Sec. 111 incident reporting: strike it.**

Describe what it does: requires every frontier developer (a trained/initiated training of a frontier model; the draft defines frontier model as a foundation model trained with more than 10^26 computational operations, and frontier developer at more than $50 million in gross revenue) to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to law enforcement where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. "Critical safety incident" includes unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, failure of the model's risk-mitigation measures, and loss of control of the model.

Then our opposition: three problems.
(a) Premise. Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, released June 4. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will decide whether the United States leads this technology or licenses it from someone else.

ACIA filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025. We made three arguments then: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. This draft takes the first argument seriously, and we commend you both for it. As you wrote in June, "policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it's written by both parties." We respond in that spirit.

Our recommendations, in brief:

1. Support Sec. 121, the preemption of state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. Delete the three-year sunset and make the provision permanent.
2. Strike the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111.
3. Strike Sec. 102, which codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year for it, and ask appropriators to defund the center.
4. Convert the remaining frontier obligations in Secs. 111 and 112, the published frameworks, transparency reports and mandatory audits, into voluntary, industry-led practice.
5. Enact and fund the draft's research, cybersecurity and infrastructure provisions.

**I. The patchwork is already costing our members real money**

Three frontier-AI statutes now bind our industry. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) has been in effect since Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by Chapter 96 of 2026, signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, Public Act 104-0538), signed July 6, follows on the same schedule, with audit obligations beginning in 2028.

In August we surveyed our members on what this costs. Eighty-six companies responded, and the figures below are aggregate; ACIA does not disclose individual responses.

- Sixty-one percent of members named conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem.
- Developers above $500 million in revenue spend a median $1.4 million a year maintaining a published frontier safety framework.
- Complying with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel consumes a median 6.5 full-time employees at affected developers.
- Thirty-four percent of our startup members report delaying a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

These are real costs paid by real companies before any federal standard exists. They are the costs of fifty potential definitions of "frontier," fifty incident-reporting timelines and fifty audit regimes. One national standard would eliminate most of them. That is the strongest case for this legislation, and we make it first.

**II. Sec. 121: right design, wrong sunset**

We support Sec. 121. The draft preempts state laws and regulations that specifically regulate the development of an AI model, defined as the acts performed or directed by a developer prior to deployment. That line is well drawn. States keep their authority over use and deployment, over products and services built on top of models, and their common-law remedies and laws of general applicability. This is a far more defensible design than the broad moratorium the Senate stripped from reconciliation by a 99-to-1 vote in July 2025.

Make it permanent. Three reasons.

First, investment certainty. Data-center buildouts are multiyear commitments, frequently financed a decade out. A preemption that expires in 2029, and must be reauthorized in a future Congress, does not change the planning math of anyone building in California or New York today.

Second, policy coherence. The executive branch has already moved. The Dec. 11, 2025 executive order established the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws that burden interstate commerce, and directed Commerce to identify conflicting state laws. The March 20, 2026 White House framework asked Congress for "a minimally burdensome national standard," "not fifty discordant ones." A temporary preemption answers that request with a shrug.

Third, a sunset is a lobbying cliff. It schedules the same fight for 2029, with the same advocates, and gives every statehouse reason to keep drafting.

**III. Sec. 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate**

Section 111 would require every frontier developer to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. "Frontier developer" reaches companies with as little as $50 million in revenue. A "critical safety incident" includes unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, a failure of the model's risk-mitigation measures, and "loss of control" of a model. The obligations are backed by civil penalties reported at up to $1 million per day.

We ask you to strike this mandate. Three problems, in order.

The premise is unfounded. ACIA's board-reviewed position is that claims of catastrophic or existential risk from AI are unsupported. No evidence shows that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations, amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, with outsized influence on AI policy in Washington. A federal reporting regime keyed to "loss of control" writes speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code. Notably, the draft's definition does not even require that actual harm occur, a broader trigger than the state statutes it displaces.

The costs are real and the scope is broad. Our developers report a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before ongoing staffing. The mandate applies to companies an order of magnitude smaller than the "large frontier developers" whose frameworks the state laws target.

It recreates the patchwork it preempts. Section 121 displaces state development regimes; Section 111 then re-imposes their substance nationwide and routes the reports to a new federal office. That is not one national standard. It is fifty sets of obligations replaced by one, plus a federal regulator.

Security incidents involving model weights are serious, and our members handle them today as security incidents, under company incident-response practices, voluntary coordination with federal cybersecurity agencies and existing criminal law. The draft supports that model elsewhere. Section 311, which we support, funds open-source security maintenance and asks large frontier developers to provide security tools to the maintainers who need them. Keep incident handling there.

**IV. Secs. 102 and 112: do not build a permanent frontier regulator**

Section 102 codifies CAISI and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, roughly 10 times the center's current appropriation of about $15 million, with additional fee authority and special pay authority above standard government pay scales. Section 112 would have that office license "independent verification organizations" to audit large frontier developers semi-annually and on the director's demand, to review their compliance and the adequacy of their frameworks for "achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks," to report to the director, and to refer violations to the attorney general and state attorneys general, mandatorily where they find "imminent catastrophic risk."

Strike both. The center already exists by executive action; Secretary Lutnick announced its creation on June 3, 2025, as a reform of the AI Safety Institute, and the July 23, 2025 AI Action Plan executive order already directs NIST's AI work. Codification is unnecessary. A new, self-funding enforcement office, with a licensing chokepoint over its own audit industry and mandatory referral powers premised on speculative doomsday scenarios, is regulatory capture waiting to happen.

NIST should return to its core measurement-science mission, as the director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy put it in July 2025: NIST needs "to go back to basics" on standards. We will make the same request of the Appropriations Committees: do not fund the codification, and return the resources to NIST's measurement programs.

**V. What ACIA supports**

The draft does far more than regulate frontier developers, and most of it deserves to move.

- Sec. 301, reauthorizing the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035.
- Sec. 311, grants to maintainers of critical open-source software.
- Secs. 122 and 321, GAO reviews of AI adoption risks and of model-weight, data-center and open-source security.
- Secs. 401 through 403, the joint Energy, NIST and NSF testbed program, including public red-teaming.
- Sec. 411, international standards coalitions with like-minded partners, excluding the People's Republic of China.
- Secs. 421 through 424, public data for AI, grand challenges, codification of the National AI Research Resource, and liquid-cooling research and development.
- Secs. 131 and 132, penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and for AI impersonation of federal officials.
- Sec. 141, limits on government pressure directed at AI platforms.
- Title II's workforce data and education programs.

Enforce these against real harms, fund the testbeds and the research resource, and keep the standards work voluntary and industry-led. That bill would have ACIA's full support.

**VI. Conclusion**

Our members will keep investing in safety whether or not Washington requires it: they publish frameworks, they test their systems, and they spend real money doing both. What they cannot do alone is fifty compliance regimes for one national industry. This draft, fixed along the lines above, can end the patchwork without building the regulator the safety-advocacy network has sought for years.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staff, and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, ahead of introduction. Our policy team, led by Vice President for Policy Tessa Marchetti, stands ready.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

{"content": "# One national standard, not a federalized patchwork

**ACIA comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)**
For Energy and Commerce member offices. October 2026. Draft, not for distribution.

**Who we are.** ACIA is a Washington, D.C. coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms.

**Where we stand.** We support the draft's preemption of state AI-development laws and most of its research and cybersecurity provisions. We oppose the incident-reporting mandate and the CAISI codification. Pass the framework, take the mandates out.

## Five asks

1. **Make preemption permanent (Sec. 121).** The draft preempts state laws that specifically regulate AI model development, then sunsets after three years. A sunset is a 2029 compliance cliff. States keep full authority over deployment and use. Make the national standard durable.

2. **Strike incident reporting (Sec. 111).** Every frontier developer above $50 million in revenue would report "critical safety incidents," including "loss of control," to a federal office within 15 days, on pain of civil penalties. The premise is unfounded, the trigger requires no actual harm, and affected members report a median $310,000 one-time cost just to stand up the function.

3. **Strike the CAISI codification (Sec. 102).** $100 million a year, roughly 10 times current funding, plus fee authority and above-scale hiring, for an office that would license the auditors who police our industry. That is regulatory capture with a budget line. Ask appropriators to defund it.

4. **Keep audits voluntary (Sec. 112).** Semi-annual mandatory audits by government-licensed verification firms would federalize the very state regime the bill preempts. Audits should remain an industry-led practice, as our members conduct them today.

5. **Fund the rest.** Sec. 301 (Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization through fiscal 2035), Sec. 311 (open-source security grants), Secs. 401-403 (AI testbeds and public red-teaming), Sec. 423 (National AI Research Resource) and Sec. 424 (liquid-cooling R&D) deserve support and full funding.

## By the numbers

ACIA member survey, August 2026. Aggregate figures, 86 respondents.

- 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.
- 34% of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months.
- 6.5 FTEs: median staffing needed to comply with California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act in parallel.
- $1.4 million: median annual cost of maintaining a published frontier safety framework.

**Contact.** Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance.", "path": "/workspace/out/hill_one_pager.md"}

[INTERNAL DRAFT. Prepared by the ACIA policy team Oct. 16, 2026, for President & CEO review and sign-off Friday, Oct. 23. Do not transmit. On sign-off, re-date and send to GAAIA@mail.house.gov the week of Oct. 26.]

---

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
Washington, D.C.

Oct. 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, released June 4. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will decide whether the United States leads this technology or licenses it from someone else.

ACIA filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025. We made three arguments then: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. This draft takes the first argument seriously, and we commend you both for it. As you wrote in June, "policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it's written by both parties." We respond in that spirit.

Our recommendations, in brief:

1. Support Sec. 121, which preempts state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. Delete the three-year sunset and make the provision permanent.
2. Strike the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111.
3. Strike Sec. 102, which codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year for it, and ask appropriators to defund the center.
4. Convert the remaining frontier obligations in Secs. 111 and 112, the published frameworks, transparency reports and mandatory audits, into voluntary, industry-led practice.
5. Enact and fund the draft's research, cybersecurity and infrastructure provisions.

**I. The patchwork is already costing our members real money**

Three frontier-AI statutes now shape our industry's compliance planning. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) has been in effect since Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by Chapter 96 of 2026, signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, Public Act 104-0538), signed July 6, follows on the same schedule, with audit obligations beginning in 2028.

In August we surveyed our members on what this costs. Eighty-six companies responded, and the figures below are aggregate; ACIA does not disclose individual responses.

- Sixty-one percent of members named conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem.
- Among our developer members above $500 million in revenue, maintaining a published frontier safety framework costs a median $1.4 million a year.
- Complying with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel consumes a median 6.5 full-time employees at affected developers.
- Thirty-four percent of our startup members report delaying a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

Those are real costs, paid by real companies, before any federal standard exists. They are the costs of dozens of possible definitions of "frontier," dozens of incident-reporting timelines and dozens of audit regimes. One national standard would eliminate most of them. That is the strongest case for this legislation, and we lead with it.

**II. Sec. 121: the right design, the wrong sunset**

We support Sec. 121. The draft preempts state laws and regulations that specifically regulate the development of an AI model, with development defined as the acts performed or directed by a developer prior to deployment. That line is well drawn. States keep their authority over use and deployment, over products and services built on top of models, and their common-law remedies and laws of general applicability. It is a far more defensible design than the broad moratorium the Senate stripped from reconciliation by a 99-to-1 vote in July 2025.

Make it permanent, for three reasons.

First, investment certainty. Data-center buildouts are multiyear commitments, frequently financed a decade out. A preemption that expires in 2029 and must survive a future reauthorization fight changes no one's planning math in California or New York today.

Second, policy coherence. The executive branch has already moved. The Dec. 11, 2025 executive order established the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws that burden interstate commerce, and directed Commerce to identify conflicting state laws. The March 20, 2026 White House framework asked Congress for "a minimally burdensome national standard," "not fifty discordant ones." A preemption with an expiration date answers that request with a shrug.

Third, a sunset is a lobbying cliff. It schedules the same fight, with the same advocates, for 2029, and it gives every statehouse a reason to keep drafting in the meantime.

**III. Sec. 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate**

Section 111 would require every frontier developer to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. The draft defines a frontier model by a compute threshold of more than 10^26 operations and a frontier developer at more than $50 million in gross revenue, so the mandate reaches well below the largest labs. A "critical safety incident" includes unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, a failure of the model's risk-mitigation measures, and loss of control of a model. The obligations carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per day of violation, enforceable by the attorney general and, in some circumstances, state attorneys general.

We ask you to strike this mandate. Three problems, in order.

The premise is unfounded. ACIA's board-reviewed position is that claims of catastrophic or existential risk from AI are unsupported. No evidence shows that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations, amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, with outsized influence on AI policy in Washington. A federal reporting regime keyed to "loss of control" writes speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code. Notably, the draft's definition does not even require that actual harm occur, a broader trigger than the state statutes it displaces.

The costs are real and the scope is broad. Our developers report a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before ongoing staffing. The mandate applies to companies far smaller than the "large frontier developers" whose frameworks the state laws target.

It recreates the patchwork it preempts. Section 121 displaces state development regimes; Section 111 then re-imposes their substance nationwide and routes the reports to a new federal office. That is not one national standard. It is fifty sets of obligations replaced by one, plus a new federal regulator to administer them.

Security incidents involving model weights are serious, and our members handle them today as security incidents: under company incident-response practices, voluntary coordination with federal cybersecurity agencies, and existing criminal law. The draft supports that model elsewhere. Section 311, which we support, funds open-source security maintenance and directs large frontier developers to give critical maintainers access to advanced AI models that can find and fix vulnerabilities. Keep incident handling there.

**IV. Secs. 102 and 112: do not build a permanent frontier regulator**

Section 102 codifies CAISI and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, an order of magnitude above the center's current appropriation of roughly $15 million, with added fee authority and special pay authority above standard government pay scales. Section 112 would have that office license "independent verification organizations" to audit large frontier developers semi-annually and on the director's demand, to assess their compliance and the adequacy of their frameworks for "achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks," to report to the director, and to refer violations to the attorney general and state attorneys general, mandatorily where they find "imminent catastrophic risk."

Strike both. The center already exists by executive action; Secretary Lutnick announced it on June 3, 2025 as a reform of the AI Safety Institute, and the July 23, 2025 AI Action Plan executive order already directs NIST's AI work. Codification is unnecessary. A new, well-funded enforcement office, holding a licensing chokepoint over its own audit industry and wielding referral powers premised on speculative doomsday scenarios, is regulatory capture waiting to happen.

NIST should return to its core measurement-science mission, as the director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy put it in July 2025: NIST needs "to go back to basics" on standards. We will make the same request of the Appropriations Committees: do not fund the codification, and return the resources to NIST's measurement programs.

**V. What ACIA supports**

The draft does far more than regulate frontier developers, and most of it deserves to move.

- Sec. 301, reauthorizing the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035.
- Sec. 311, grants to maintainers of critical open-source software.
- Secs. 122 and 321, GAO reviews of federal AI adoption and of model-weight, data-center and open-source security.
- Secs. 401 through 403, the joint Energy, NIST and NSF testbed program, including public red-teaming.
- Sec. 411, international standards coalitions with like-minded partners that counter foreign adversary influence.
- Secs. 421 through 424, public data for AI, grand challenges, codification of the National AI Research Resource, and liquid-cooling research and development.
- Secs. 131 and 132, penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and for AI impersonation of federal officials.
- Sec. 141, limits on government pressure directed at AI platforms.
- Title II's workforce data and education programs.

Enforce against real harms, fund the testbeds and the research resource, and keep the standards work voluntary and industry-led. That bill would have ACIA's full support.

**VI. Conclusion**

Our members will keep investing in safety whether or not Washington requires it. They publish frameworks, they test their systems, and they spend real money doing both. What they cannot do alone is run dozens of compliance regimes for one national industry. This draft, fixed along the lines above, can end the patchwork without building the regulator that the safety-advocacy network has sought for years.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staff, and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, ahead of introduction. Our policy team, led by Vice President for Policy Tessa Marchetti, stands ready.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
