# GAAIA discussion draft: ACIA asks by section

Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, discussion draft released June 4, 2026, by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA). Section numbers follow the sponsors' section-by-section summary and the draft table of contents.

Positions marked "support" or "oppose" reflect the board-approved ACIA messaging guide (v4, Sept. 30, 2026). Positions on sections the guide does not address are drafted from ACIA's March 2025 OSTP AI Action Plan comment and flagged for confirmation by the VP for Policy.

| Draft provision | ACIA position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 101, definitions ("critical safety incident," "catastrophic risk," "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation") | Oppose | Strike the defined terms along with the mandates they serve | The definitions write speculative doomsday scenarios into law. |
| Sec. 102, CAISI codification; $100M per year, FY2027-2029; fee and special-pay authority | Oppose | Strike Sec. 102 and the authorization; ask appropriators to defund CAISI | A permanently funded standards office with licensing power over its own auditors is regulatory capture. |
| Sec. 111, frontier AI framework mandate (large frontier developers) | Oppose the mandate, support voluntary publication | Strike the mandate; keep framework publication voluntary | Covered members already spend a median $1.4M a year on published frameworks. |
| Sec. 111, transparency reports (all frontier developers) | Oppose the mandate | Strike, or fold into voluntary disclosure | A federal reporting layer re-imports what Sec. 121 preempts. |
| Sec. 111, critical-safety-incident reporting (15 days to the CAISI director; 24 hours to law enforcement if imminent risk) | Oppose | Strike the incident-reporting requirement | A median $310,000 one-time cost for a regime premised on unfounded loss-of-control scenarios. |
| Sec. 112, CAISI-licensed independent verification organization audits (semi-annual plus on demand; referrals to DOJ and state AGs) | Oppose | Strike; audits remain voluntary and industry-led | Government-licensed auditors with referral power create a captive audit industry. |
| Sec. 113, anti-retaliation protections for AI whistleblowers | No formal position | None at this time | Not addressed in the board-approved messaging guide; pending member input. |
| Sec. 121, preemption of state laws specifically regulating AI model development; three-year sunset | Support with changes | Delete the sunset; make preemption permanent | One national standard, not a patchwork that costs covered developers a median 6.5 FTEs. |
| Secs. 131-132, AI-enabled financial crimes; AI impersonation of federal officials | Support | As drafted | Enforcement should target real harms, not model development. |
| Sec. 141, limits on government pressure directed at AI platforms | Support | As drafted | Free-speech protections keep development decisions with developers, not with officials. |
| Title II, workforce data and education programs | Support in principle | Under review | Labor-market data is useful; ACIA is reviewing the subtitle's reporting details. |
| Sec. 301, reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035 | Support | As drafted | A decade of threat sharing has worked; give it certainty. |
| Sec. 311, grants for designated critical open-source software maintainers | Support | As drafted; fund fully | Open-source maintainers secure the software stack our industry runs on. |
| Secs. 122 and 321, GAO reviews (federal AI adoption; model-weight, data-center and open-source security) | Support | As drafted | Independent measurement, not mission creep. |
| Secs. 401-403, joint Energy, NIST and NSF testbed program, public red-teaming and hackathon | Support | As drafted; fund | Public evaluation beats private mandates. |
| Sec. 411, international standards coalitions with like-minded partners | Support | As drafted | U.S.-led standards, not adversary-led ones. |
| Secs. 421-424, public data for AI, grand challenges, NAIRR codification, liquid-cooling R&D | Support | As drafted; fund | Matches our March 2025 ask to unlock compute and energy. |

The Honorable Lori Trahan
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, released June 4. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will decide whether the United States leads this technology or licenses it from someone else.

ACIA filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025. We made three arguments then: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. This draft takes the first argument seriously, and we commend you both for it. As you wrote in June, "policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it's written by both parties." We respond in that spirit.

Our recommendations, in brief:

1. Support Sec. 121, which preempts state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. Delete the three-year sunset and make the provision permanent.
2. Strike the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111.
3. Strike Sec. 102, which codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year for it, and ask appropriators to defund the center.
4. Convert the remaining frontier obligations in Secs. 111 and 112, the published frameworks, transparency reports and mandatory audits, into voluntary, industry-led practice.
5. Enact and fund the draft's research, cybersecurity and infrastructure provisions.

**I. The patchwork is already costing our members real money**

Three frontier-AI statutes now shape our industry's compliance planning. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) has been in effect since Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by Chapter 96 of 2026, signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, Public Act 104-0538), signed July 6, follows on the same schedule, with audit obligations beginning in 2028.

In August we surveyed our members on what this costs. Eighty-six companies responded, and the figures below are aggregate; ACIA does not disclose individual responses.

- Sixty-one percent of members named conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem.
- Among our developer members above $500 million in revenue, maintaining a published frontier safety framework costs a median $1.4 million a year.
- Complying with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel consumes a median 6.5 full-time employees at affected developers.
- Thirty-four percent of our startup members report delaying a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

Those are real costs, paid by real companies, before any federal standard exists. They are the costs of dozens of possible definitions of "frontier," dozens of incident-reporting timelines and dozens of audit regimes. One national standard would eliminate most of them. That is the strongest case for this legislation, and we lead with it.

**II. Sec. 121: the right design, the wrong sunset**

We support Sec. 121. The draft preempts state laws and regulations that specifically regulate the development of an AI model, with development defined as the acts performed or directed by a developer prior to deployment. That line is well drawn. States keep their authority over use and deployment, over products and services built on top of models, and their common-law remedies and laws of general applicability. It is a far more defensible design than the broad moratorium the Senate stripped from reconciliation by a 99-to-1 vote in July 2025.

Make it permanent, for three reasons.

First, investment certainty. Data-center buildouts are multiyear commitments, frequently financed a decade out. A preemption that expires in 2029 and must survive a future reauthorization fight changes no one's planning math in California or New York today.

Second, policy coherence. The executive branch has already moved. The Dec. 11, 2025 executive order established the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws that burden interstate commerce, and directed Commerce to identify conflicting state laws. The March 20, 2026 White House framework asked Congress for "a minimally burdensome national standard," "not fifty discordant ones." A preemption with an expiration date answers that request with a shrug.

Third, a sunset is a lobbying cliff. It schedules the same fight, with the same advocates, for 2029, and it gives every statehouse a reason to keep drafting in the meantime.

**III. Sec. 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate**

Section 111 would require every frontier developer to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. The draft defines a frontier model by a compute threshold of more than 10^26 operations and a frontier developer at more than $50 million in gross revenue, so the mandate reaches well below the largest labs. A "critical safety incident" includes unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, a failure of the model's risk-mitigation measures, and loss of control of a model. The obligations carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per day of violation, enforceable by the attorney general and, in some circumstances, state attorneys general.

We ask you to strike this mandate. Three problems, in order.

The premise is unfounded. ACIA's board-reviewed position is that claims of catastrophic or existential risk from AI are unsupported. No evidence shows that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations, amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, with outsized influence on AI policy in Washington. A federal reporting regime keyed to "loss of control" writes speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code. Notably, the draft's definition does not even require that actual harm occur, a broader trigger than the state statutes it displaces.

The costs are real and the scope is broad. Our developers report a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before ongoing staffing. The mandate applies to companies far smaller than the "large frontier developers" whose frameworks the state laws target.

It recreates the patchwork it preempts. Section 121 displaces state development regimes; Section 111 then re-imposes their substance nationwide and routes the reports to a new federal office. That is not one national standard. It is fifty sets of obligations replaced by one, plus a new federal regulator to administer them.

Security incidents involving model weights are serious, and our members handle them today as security incidents: under company incident-response practices, voluntary coordination with federal cybersecurity agencies, and existing criminal law. The draft supports that model elsewhere. Section 311, which we support, funds open-source security maintenance and directs large frontier developers to give critical maintainers access to advanced AI models that can find and fix vulnerabilities. Keep incident handling there.

**IV. Secs. 102 and 112: do not build a permanent frontier regulator**

Section 102 codifies CAISI and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, an order of magnitude above the center's current appropriation of roughly $15 million, with added fee authority and special pay authority above standard government pay scales. Section 112 would have that office license "independent verification organizations" to audit large frontier developers semi-annually and on the director's demand, to assess their compliance and the adequacy of their frameworks for "achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks," to report to the director, and to refer violations to the attorney general and state attorneys general, mandatorily where they find "imminent catastrophic risk."

Strike both. The center already exists by executive action; Secretary Lutnick announced it on June 3, 2025 as a reform of the AI Safety Institute, and the July 23, 2025 AI Action Plan executive order already directs NIST's AI work. Codification is unnecessary. A new, well-funded enforcement office, holding a licensing chokepoint over its own audit industry and wielding referral powers premised on speculative doomsday scenarios, is regulatory capture waiting to happen.

NIST should return to its core measurement-science mission, as the director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy put it in July 2025: NIST needs "to go back to basics" on standards. We will make the same request of the Appropriations Committees: do not fund the codification, and return the resources to NIST's measurement programs.

**V. What ACIA supports**

The draft does far more than regulate frontier developers, and most of it deserves to move.

- Sec. 301, reauthorizing the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035.
- Sec. 311, grants to maintainers of critical open-source software.
- Secs. 122 and 321, GAO reviews of federal AI adoption and of model-weight, data-center and open-source security.
- Secs. 401 through 403, the joint Energy, NIST and NSF testbed program, including public red-teaming.
- Sec. 411, international standards coalitions with like-minded partners that counter foreign adversary influence.
- Secs. 421 through 424, public data for AI, grand challenges, codification of the National AI Research Resource, and liquid-cooling research and development.
- Secs. 131 and 132, penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and for AI impersonation of federal officials.
- Sec. 141, limits on government pressure directed at AI platforms.
- Title II's workforce data and education programs.

Enforce against real harms, fund the testbeds and the research resource, and keep the standards work voluntary and industry-led. That bill would have ACIA's full support.

**VI. Conclusion**

Our members will keep investing in safety whether or not Washington requires it. They publish frameworks, they test their systems, and they spend real money doing both. What they cannot do alone is run dozens of compliance regimes for one national industry. This draft, fixed along the lines above, can end the patchwork without building the regulator that the safety-advocacy network has sought for years.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staff, and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, ahead of introduction. Our policy team, led by Vice President for Policy Tessa Marchetti, stands ready.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# One national standard, not a federalized patchwork

**ACIA comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)**
For Energy and Commerce member offices. October 2026. Draft, not for distribution.

**Who we are.** ACIA is a Washington, D.C. coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms.

**Where we stand.** We support the draft's preemption of state AI-development laws and most of its research and cybersecurity provisions. We oppose the incident-reporting mandate and the CAISI codification. Pass the framework, take the mandates out.

## Five asks

1. **Make preemption permanent (Sec. 121).** The draft preempts state laws that specifically regulate AI model development, then sunsets after three years. A sunset is a 2029 compliance cliff. States keep full authority over deployment and use. Make the national standard durable.

2. **Strike incident reporting (Sec. 111).** Every frontier developer above $50 million in revenue would report "critical safety incidents," including "loss of control," to a federal office within 15 days, on pain of civil penalties. The premise is unfounded, the trigger requires no actual harm, and affected members report a median $310,000 one-time cost just to stand up the function.

3. **Strike the CAISI codification (Sec. 102).** $100 million a year, roughly 10 times current funding, plus fee authority and above-scale hiring, for an office that would license the auditors who police our industry. That is regulatory capture with a budget line. Ask appropriators to defund it.

4. **Keep audits voluntary (Sec. 112).** Semi-annual mandatory audits by government-licensed verification firms would federalize the very state regime the bill preempts. Audits should remain an industry-led practice, as our members conduct them today.

5. **Fund the rest.** Sec. 301 (Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization through fiscal 2035), Sec. 311 (open-source security grants), Secs. 401-403 (AI testbeds and public red-teaming), Sec. 423 (National AI Research Resource) and Sec. 424 (liquid-cooling R&D) deserve support and full funding.

## By the numbers

ACIA member survey, August 2026. Aggregate figures, 86 respondents.

- 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.
- 34% of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months.
- 6.5 FTEs: median staffing needed to comply with California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act in parallel.
- $1.4 million: median annual cost of maintaining a published frontier safety framework.

**Contact.** Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance.

# Staff Q&A: GAAIA discussion draft

Answers to anticipated questions from September 2026 Hill meetings, aligned to the board-approved messaging guide (v4). Each answer is 120 words or fewer. Spokesperson: ACIA policy team.

## 1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."

They answer different questions. We support preemption because development is a national activity, and conflicting state regimes cost our affected developers a median 6.5 full-time employees each. That is a jurisdictional judgment. Incident reporting is a substantive mandate we oppose on the merits, and it is not lighter: GAAIA extends reporting to every frontier developer above $50 million in revenue, firms SB 53 never reached, and its trigger, unlike the state statutes, requires no actual harm. Members report a median $310,000 one-time cost just to stand up the function. A lighter version of a mandate built on unfounded premises is still a mandate built on unfounded premises.

## 2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"

Voluntary ones, backed by real federal capacity. Our members publish safety frameworks today, spending a median $1.4 million a year to maintain them, and they red-team, evaluate and coordinate with federal cybersecurity agencies. We support the draft's testbed program and public red-teaming (Secs. 401-403), GAO's model-weight security reviews (Secs. 122 and 321), CISA's open-source security grants (Sec. 311), and enforcement against real harms like AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of officials (Secs. 131-132). What we cannot accept is mandatory reporting and audits premised on "loss of control," or a codified $100 million a year regulator to administer them. Keep it to measurement science at NIST.

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent? What's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"

Permanent. Three years answers a fifty-state patchwork with a countdown clock. Our data-center members finance buildouts over multiyear horizons; a preemption that lapses in 2029, pending reauthorization, changes no one's planning. And a sunset is a lobbying cliff: it schedules the same fight, with the same advocates, two Congresses from now. We recognize the sensitivity after the Senate removed the broad ten-year moratorium by a 99-to-1 vote in July 2025. That is exactly why the draft's narrower design, development activities only, with states keeping deployment and use authority, is the right scope. Durability is the point. A standard that expires is a standard that never existed.

## 4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million per year. What's your view on the funding level?"

Zero. Strike Sec. 102 and its authorization. CAISI exists by executive action, created in June 2025, and can stay that way; codification buys nothing but permanence for a mandate machine. The $100 million a year is roughly ten times the center's current appropriation, before fee authority and above-scale hiring, and it would license the auditors who police our industry, with mandatory referrals to the Justice Department premised on "imminent catastrophic risk." Our request to appropriators: do not fund it, and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. That is the same standard the White House's own science office set in 2025: back to basics.
